auditor.definition: Independently reviews and verifies that the security program actually matches the policy, and reports findings to those in charge. Inspects and reports — never fixes what it finds, or independence is gone.

board.definition: Governs on behalf of the owners of the organization: provides oversight of executive management, demands evidence of due care and due diligence, and holds the executives to account for risk — without running the program itself.

ciso.definition: Holds functional, not ultimate, responsibility: drafts the security policy and standards, designs and runs the control program on management's behalf, and reports its state upward. Implements direction rather than owning the liability.

coa-01.text: After a costly breach, regulators ask who in the organization can be shown to have exercised due care over the security program as a whole. One seat answers.
coa-01.why: Ultimate responsibility and legal liability for security sit with senior management; delegating the work never delegates the accountability.

coa-02.text: The new information security policy is finished, but until one signature lands on it, nobody is obliged to follow it.
coa-02.why: A policy carries authority only once senior management endorses it — the security team can write it, but cannot make it binding.

coa-03.text: A risk assessment leaves residual risk on the table that no control will treat. Someone must formally decide the organization will live with it.
coa-03.why: Accepting residual risk is a business decision reserved for the level that owns the consequences — senior management, not the security function.

coa-04.text: Shareholders want assurance that executive management is being held to account for cyber risk, not merely trusted to manage it.
coa-04.why: The board governs on the owners' behalf: it oversees and challenges executive management rather than operating the program.

coa-05.text: A quarterly session where the CEO is questioned on the organization's risk posture and must show evidence, not reassurance.
coa-05.why: Demanding evidence of due care and due diligence from the executives is board-level oversight in action.

coa-06.text: Chartering an independent committee whose review of the security program deliberately bypasses the management chain it examines.
coa-06.why: Standing up independent oversight structures is a governance act — it belongs to the body that supervises management, not to management itself.

coa-07.text: Someone must turn the executives' risk appetite into a written security policy, with standards and baselines hanging beneath it.
coa-07.why: Writing the policy and the documents under it is the security professional's functional responsibility — management directs and endorses, the professional drafts.

coa-08.text: Designing the control program that will implement the endorsed policy, and running it day to day on management's behalf.
coa-08.why: The security professional implements management's security direction — functional responsibility for making the program real.

coa-09.text: Compiling the security program's metrics and reporting its true state up the chain so executives can answer for it.
coa-09.why: The security function is management's implementer and informer: it must surface program state to the level that carries the liability.

coa-10.text: A newly assembled research dataset needs a sensitivity level before any handling rule can apply to it. Someone must set that level.
coa-10.why: Classifying the asset is the owner's defining duty — the classification decision drives every protection that follows.

coa-11.text: A project team requests access to the customer database. The request needs a decision from whoever answers for that data.
coa-11.why: Deciding who may access an asset belongs to its owner; administrators merely carry out the grant the owner approves.

coa-12.text: The finance department head delegated every protection task for the ledger system months ago — yet when its protection fails, this person still answers.
coa-12.why: An owner delegates tasks to custodians but keeps accountability for the asset's protection — the delegation moves work, not answerability.

coa-13.text: Running the nightly backup of the file server and periodically proving the restore actually works.
coa-13.why: Backing up and restoring data is the day-to-day protection work delegated to the custodian by the owner and the policy.

coa-14.text: Applying the correct sensitivity markings to a batch of media, exactly as the classification scheme prescribes.
coa-14.why: The custodian applies the labels; the level being marked was decided elsewhere, by the owner. Doing is custodial, deciding is not.

coa-15.text: Implementing the specific safeguards the security policy prescribes for a data store — configured, maintained, and kept running.
coa-15.why: Implementing prescribed protection is the custodian's charter: hands-on execution of rules that management and the policy defined.

coa-16.text: Determining whether the controls actually deployed across the estate match what the written policy claims, and putting the gap in writing.
coa-16.why: Reviewing and verifying that the policy is properly implemented — and reporting on it — is precisely the auditor's role.

coa-17.text: During a compliance review, a tester finds a misconfigured control and is tempted to quietly correct it on the spot. The role forbids it.
coa-17.why: An auditor who remediates what they inspect has destroyed their own independence; they report findings for others to fix.

coa-18.text: Producing the periodic report that tells governance whether the security program's practice matches its paperwork.
coa-18.why: Independent verification reported upward is the auditor's product — it is how the accountable layers learn the truth.

coa-19.text: Locking the workstation when stepping away and refusing to share a password with a colleague on deadline.
coa-19.why: Following policy and protecting credentials in daily work is every user's obligation — no special role required.

coa-20.text: Spotting a suspicious email and reporting it through the published procedure instead of deleting it and moving on.
coa-20.why: Users are obliged to follow the organization's procedures, including reporting suspected security events they encounter.

coa-21.text: Working all day with sensitive records while touching only the data the job actually requires — and nothing more.
coa-21.why: Operating within least privilege and handling data per its classification is the user's share of the accountability chain.

coa-matrix.prompt: Accountability follows the org chart, not the keyboard. For each duty, ask who ANSWERS for it — not who touches the system that performs it.

custodian.definition: Delegated the hands-on protection tasks the owner and policy prescribe: backups, storage, labeling, restoration and other day-to-day care of the asset — responsible for doing the work, not for choosing the rules.

dataowner.definition: Usually a senior business figure accountable for a specific asset: decides its classification, decides who may access it, and remains answerable for its protection even while delegating the daily work.

seniormgmt.definition: Carries ultimate organizational responsibility and liability for security. Signs the policy that gives it authority, sets the risk appetite, and formally accepts whatever risk remains — accountability that cannot be delegated away.

users.definition: Everyone who touches systems and data to do their job: obliged to follow policy and procedures, guard their credentials, handle information per its classification, and operate under least privilege.
